lesson.title: Eszett & the Sharp S
lesson.subtitle: groß, Straße, muss — the T→SS story you can now read letter by letter

hook.title: The Letter English Deleted
hook.content: That letter that looks like a strange B — ß — is not a B at all. Germans call it Eszett: 'S-z'. It is a sharp S, and it exists because of the shift you already know. When an ancient t hissed into s after a long vowel, German wrote the hiss as ß: groß (great), heiß (hot), Fuß (foot), Straße (street). After a short vowel, the same hiss is written double-s: Wasser, besser, muss. English deleted its sharp s centuries ago and let the plain s do both jobs — German kept the specialist.

footnotes.title: The Country That Abolished It
footnotes.content: Switzerland stopped using ß in the 1930s and writes ss everywhere. So 'ss' and 'ß' are pure spelling tradition — the sound is the same sharp [s]. Austria and Germany kept the long/short distinction.

pattern.title: The Sharp-S Spelling Compass
pattern.content: Long vowel or diphthong → ß: groß, heiß, Fuß, Straße, weiß (white — the same word as wise: ich weiß, I know, is 'I am wise'). Short vowel → ss: Wasser, besser, muss, muss's du-form musst. The shift underneath never changes: water → Wasser (t → ss), better → besser (tt → ss), foot → Fuß (t → ß). Ordering drinks now needs no new words: ein Glas Wasser, and when it is too hot, zu heiß. Salt, Salz, is the t → z twin of English salt — one more member of the same sibilant family.
pattern.linguist_note: Straße carries the full Roman history: Latin via strata ('paved road') gave English street (keeping Latin t) and German Straße (shifting t to ß). The same road produced both words on two sides of the Rhine.

exercises.prompt: Match the English t-words with their sharp-s German twins:
exercises.target_answer: groß, heiß, Fuß, Straße, süß, Zunge
exercises.meaning: great/big, hot, foot, street, sweet, tongue
exercises.explanation: Each ß marks where an ancient t hissed into a sharp s after a long vowel — and Zunge shows the sibling outcome: t → z, the /ts/ costume.

exercises.prompt: When does German write ß instead of ss?
exercises.meaning: Long vowel → ß; short vowel → ss
exercises.explanation: groß, heiß, Fuß (long) versus Wasser, muss (short). The sound is the same; the spelling tracks the vowel. Run your shelf while you're here — der Mund and der Darm from topic 4, der Monat too: none of them needs a new sound, only the flags you already collected.

exercises.prompt: Which English adjective meaning 'total / flagrant' (or 'twelve dozen') is the T/SS→S twin of 'groß'?
exercises.explanation: English gross kept the old sense 'big, total' in gross income and a gross error — no yuck factor involved.

exercises.prompt: Conjugate: 'Ich muss, du _____' (the sharp double-s du-form):
exercises.explanation: Short vowel, so the spelling doubles the s: musst. The sound never changed.

vocab_hints.note: das Kleid — the dress you met through its hardened th

exercises.explanation: zu does double duty — 'to' and 'too' — and groß wears the sharp S of its ancient t, the word English kept as gross.

summary.outcome: Read ß as a shifted t, spell musst correctly, and complain about clothes and drinks.
summary.takeaway: ß is the written receipt of T→SS after long vowels; after short vowels German writes ss.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the Velar Shift — how English make melted into machen and book into Buch.

twist.prompt: Same dress, different verdict: it isn't too big after all. Negate it.
twist.target_answer: Das Kleid ist nicht zu groß
twist.explanation: nicht slides in before the phrase it cancels — here the whole zu groß. ist holds position 2 either way.

groß.etymology_derivation: T → S/ß shift from Germanic "great". Preserved in English "gross income", "gross national product", and "a gross error" (large, not disgusting).

straße.etymology_derivation: Roman paved road (via strata) gave English "street" (kept Latin "t") and German "Straße" (shifted "t" to sharp "ß").

müssen.context_translation: I must / have to go now.
müssen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English "must" (root shifted to sibilant -ss-).

süß.context_phrase: Der Kuchen ist zu süß für mich.
süß.context_translation: The cake is too sweet for me.
süß.etymology_derivation: süß — from Proto-Germanic *swōtuz, PIE *swéh₂dus, exactly cognate with English sweet; the final t shifted to ß and the old w was lost before the rounded vowel. [wiktionary]

mund.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *munþaz — English kept the th, German hardened it to d. [wiktionary]

kleid.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *klaiþą — English cloth is the cognate: English th ↔ German d. [wiktionary]

monat.etymology_derivation: The twin of English month, from *mānōþ 'moon' (see der Mond) — th→d included. [wiktionary]

darm.context_phrase: Der Magen und der Darm verdauen das Essen.
darm.context_translation: The stomach and the intestine digest the food.

wohnzimmer.context_translation: We are sitting in the living room.
wohnzimmer.etymology_derivation: Compound of wohnen and Zimmer; Zimmer corresponds to English timber via the t to z shift. [wiktionary]

hass.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *hatis — English hate with its t became German Hass with the shifted ss, just like water became Wasser. [wiktionary]

fußgänger.context_phrase: Der Fußgänger wartet an der Ampel.
fußgänger.context_translation: The pedestrian waits at the traffic light.
fußgänger.etymology_derivation: Fuß + Gänger, both documented twins (foot, and gehen the twin of go) — a foot-goer, what Latin-based English calls a pedestrian. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
